captions.text: You maintain a Python library. In this curated example, remove duplicates without changing the caller's original list.
The input contains elm twice. The current output keeps both copies. The required output keeps the first elm, then ash and birch.
You ask for a fix. PatchProof checks the model's proposed code, then keeps the patch and results together for your review.
The original condition only compares with the previous item. The proposed condition checks every item already kept.
The model can edit solution.py. The check definitions stay outside that file; a separate runner tests the proposal.
Before repair, 5 of 9 checks passed. This proposal passes all 9, including unchanged input and TypeError for None.
A passing result covers the listed cases. You still inspect the full patch and decide whether to use it. Nothing is merged automatically.
Here is a separate repair that failed. Rows become columns, but a real null cell must stay null. The fill value is only for missing cells.
This patch still replaces null with 9. Only 11 of 13 checks pass, so it is not accepted. Later attempts had check errors.
Inspect the saved source change before using it. The added code keeps an item only when it is not already in the result.
Open an actual check: expected and observed outputs match. The recorded observations also show the original input was left unchanged.
Download the patch, requirements and recorded observations for review. These examples explain the workflow, not a benchmark advantage.
To try it yourself, choose a curated Python task and select Generate patch. It starts a new model run and checks the proposal.
Then review the patch and its results. This public demo uses curated examples; it does not accept your own repository.
